rationale: A wins because it does the harder editorial work: it names what could kill each angle before a reporter does, especially in “Calm's trial shows an 18% anxiety-score drop. The fine print is ‘regular users’ and ‘self-reported.’” B is solid, but “Free Calm Premium reaches 25 million insurance members — if they actually use it” drifts into an engagement trend angle without supplied engagement data. The gap is not huge; B has real bones. A is simply sharper, more skeptical, and more useful before anyone burns reporter trust.
gaps_in_A: “The payer-strategy question stays live for a week or so” is plausible but asserted; stronger if tied only to publication/deal timing instead of newsroom shelf-life confidence.
“one covered member willing to describe signing up” may be unavailable at announcement time, though A correctly labels that as required proof.
The four kept angles are strong, but the member service angle needs insurer names and activation steps so badly that without them it is mostly a placeholder.
gaps_in_B: “Its next 25 million users won't pay it directly” overstates the facts. The update says members get Premium at no cost, not that all 25 million become users.
“expected or historical engagement rates Calm can share” asks for useful proof, but the angle itself leans on engagement without any supplied engagement figure.
“Decay: 24hr” on the business-model angle is too timid and internally weaker than A; undisclosed economics can sustain follow-up beyond the announcement cycle.

“coverage decisions and the line between wellness perks and reimbursable health benefits” is close, but B does less than A to force the crucial distinction between a true medical-plan covered benefit and a no-cost wellness add-on.
